nefarious

nih-FAIR-ee-us -- stress on the second syllable, FAIR. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Nefarious is wicked or evil, especially in a criminal way.

The thriller's nefarious arms dealer secretly funds both sides of the war for profit.

Worked Example

In the novel, a smiling businessman runs a beloved children's charity -- and uses it as a front to steal the donations, one forged invoice at a time.

His scheme is nefarious: deliberately evil and criminal, planned with full knowledge of the harm it causes. Nefarious is for villains and their plots -- wickedness with intent behind it, not accidents or mistakes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

villainous: Villainous means befitting a villain -- a villainous sneer, a villainous landlord -- and paints the person or the role. Nefarious usually paints the deed: a nefarious scheme, plot, or purpose, wickedness that is planned and criminal. Characters are villainous; the plans they hatch are nefarious.

diabolical: Diabolical paints evil as brilliantly, fiendishly clever -- a diabolical trap worthy of a devil. Nefarious marks a scheme as wicked and criminal without requiring genius; a nefarious plot can be blunt and simple. Diabolical shows off its cleverness; nefarious only needs villainy on purpose.

underhanded: Underhanded covers everyday dishonesty done out of sight -- an underhanded deal, a trick to win a contract. Nefarious is a full shade darker: deliberately evil, usually criminal. Cheating at a neighborhood card game is underhanded; a plot to burn down a rival's warehouse is nefarious.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

honorable: upright, honest, and deserving respect

benevolent: kind and well-meaning

Where it sits · how deep the moral rot goes — wicked → nefarious → iniquitous

wicked vs. nefarious: Wicked is broad and a shade lighter than nefarious -- a wicked deed crosses a moral line, while a nefarious scheme is deliberately, criminally evil, planned in cold blood.

iniquitous vs. nefarious: Iniquitous carries even more moral weight than nefarious: a nefarious plot is wicked and criminal, while an iniquitous system is so grossly unjust that it corrupts everything and everyone it touches.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — nefari-

root — nefari-: wrong; a crime against divine law (Latin nefas 'a wrong, an impious act,' from ne- 'not' + fas 'divine law')

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: full of; possessing the qualities of (Latin -osus, via Old French -ous)

Put it together

Put it together: Nefarious uses the -ious variant of this unit's suffix family. Latin nefas named a wrong so deep it broke divine law itself -- ne- ('not') plus fas ('divine law'). Someone nefarious is literally 'full of nefas': full of wrongs that violate the most basic laws of right and wrong.

Use the root in a new word: nefariously

Use the root in a new word: nefariously: The hackers worked nefariously through the night, draining the charity's accounts.

Word Building

Word Choice

Nefarious attaches to schemes, plots, purposes, and villains -- evil that is intended. Keep it distinct from two neighbors in this unit: insidious harm creeps in unnoticed, and an egregious error is shockingly bad without needing any evil intent at all. Nefarious is the one that requires a villain.
